title: From Secret to Open • The Call from the Hill of Safa • House to House, Market to Market • The Weapon That Sheds No Blood

blocks.1: For three years the da‘wah went on quietly; house to house, to trustworthy people. Then one day the command came, now no more in hiding.
blocks.3: So proclaim openly to the people what you are commanded. (Yet) pay no heed to those who commit shirk.{{1}}
blocks.4: But where would the open da‘wah begin? Allah settled it: first of all, with the people of his own house.
blocks.6: And (O Prophet!) warn your nearest family.{{1}}
blocks.7: Why did the work begin like this! One, a man who cannot warn his own father, uncle and brother, his call sounds hollow to outsiders. Two, so that later no one could say, he frightened outsiders, yet spared his own relatives. Even for ties of blood there is no exemption.
blocks.8: The First Gathering in the Courtyard of the House
blocks.9: The Prophet {{1}} called ‘Ali (RA). He said, cook a leg of mutton. And keep a cup of milk. ‘Ali was then a youth. He worked it out and saw that this food would not fill even one man’s stomach. And forty people were invited. The men of Banu Hashim and Banu ‘Abd al-Muttalib. The uncles came. The cousins came. Abu Talib came. Hamzah came. ‘Abbas came. And Abu Lahab came too. They sat. The food came. One ate. Two ate. Ten ate. Forty rose from eating.
blocks.10: And food was still left in the vessel. ‘Ali (RA) said later, I was looking on in amazement.{{1}}
blocks.11: The meal was over. Now it was time to say the real thing. Forty men were still looking at that vessel. For what they had seen they had no explanation. The Prophet {{1}} was about to open his mouth. Just then Abu Lahab snatched the word away. He had understood that after this sight, whatever the nephew said, people would listen. So he did not give him the chance to speak. Pointing a finger at the vessel of food he raised his voice and said, this man of yours has bewitched you well. He did not say, nothing of the kind happened.
blocks.12: He could not have; everyone had seen it with their own eyes, eaten it in their own stomachs. So he did not deny the event. He gave the event a new name. Sorcery. Is this what you called us here for! Come, get up. One word. And the whole scene was wiped away. One got up. Then another. The assembly broke up. Not a single word was said.
blocks.13: The next day he called everyone again. The same food again. The same forty again. This time he began speaking right along with the eating. He said, I do not know whether any Arab youth has ever brought to his people anything better than this. I have come to you with the good of both this world and the Hereafter. And my Lord has commanded me to call you to Him. Then he asked, who will stand by my side in this work?
blocks.14: The assembly was silent. No one moved. Sitting before him were his own uncles. In whose laps he had grown up. Everyone lowered their eyes. Then from one corner of the house someone stood up. The smallest person. ‘Ali. His age then thirteen or fourteen.{{1}}
blocks.15: He said, I will stand. The Prophet {{1}} called him close. Then he said to all those present, this is my brother among you; listen to him. The people of the assembly burst out laughing. As they got up they began saying to Abu Talib, you have been told to listen to your son and obey him! But where the laughter stopped, history began from there. And he was the youngest of all. Of the forty, one had responded. And with that one the work began.{{2}}
blocks.16: Those who sat in the house that day were no ordinary men. There were uncles, there were heads of the clan, there were elders in age and experience. The one who responded was the youngest boy. We calculate from the opposite direction.
blocks.17: We think, if so-and-so were to come to the path of religion, how much work would be done. And the boy who sits beside us every day, we do not even count him. Allah did not leave it to our calculation whom He will take work from.
blocks.18: Allah commanded the open da‘wah. And where did He say to start! Not outside. From your own house. We do exactly the opposite. We give talks in the mosque, we do not give them at home. We advise strangers, and we do not advise our own son. We write on Facebook, and the person lying in the next room we do not tell.
blocks.19: Why don’t we tell! Because outsiders do not know us. They only hear the words. And the people of the house know us. Before hearing the words they look at the speaker. They know what kind of person I am.
blocks.20: Here is the real point. When the Prophet {{1}} stood in the courtyard and said to Banu Hashim, I have come to you with the good of this world and the Hereafter; the men sitting before him had known him for forty years. They had seen his childhood. They had seen his youth. They knew that this man had never told a lie. So his call did not sound hollow.
blocks.21: And why does our call sound hollow at home! We know the answer to the question. I tell my son about the prayer. And he sees that I myself do not get up for Fajr. I tell my daughter to speak the truth. And she sees that when the phone rings I say, tell them I am not at home. The word then is not a word; it is a sound.
blocks.22: And the second reason is even simpler. When one goes to give da‘wah at home there is the fear of spoiling the relationship. If an outsider gets angry he goes away. If someone at home gets angry, you have to spend the night with him. So we stay silent, and call it prudence.
blocks.23: The Prophet {{1}} did not stay silent. He knew Abu Lahab was sitting right there. He knew that if he said it the house might break apart. Yet he said it. Because to him greater than the relationship was the end of those people.
blocks.24: One more thing. There were forty men in that assembly. How many responded! One. And he was the youngest, the weakest, the one given the least importance. So if you give da‘wah at home and get no response, do not break down. Even in the first assembly of the Prophet {{1}} only one responded. And that one was enough.
blocks.25: Begin with one task. The person in your house whom you avoid the most, this week go and sit beside him once. No need to give a talk. Just sit. Da‘wah begins from there.
blocks.26: The Call from the Hill of Safa
blocks.27: One day at dawn. Makkah was just waking. The Prophet {{1}} climbed the hill of Safa. He climbed and stood on a high rock. Then he called out at the top of his voice. Ya Sabahah. This is the cry the Arabs gave when an enemy suddenly fell upon them; a danger signal of the early morning.
blocks.28: Then he called clan by clan. O Banu Fihr, O Banu ‘Adi, O Banu ‘Abd Manaf. The city shook. Wherever they were, they left everything and ran. Some in the middle of work. Some in the middle of eating. One who could not come himself sent someone. On everyone’s lips one question; what has happened! Because for an Arab not to come on hearing this call was unimaginable.
blocks.29: When everyone had gathered the Prophet {{1}} said, tell me, if I say that behind this hill a troop of horsemen is hiding, about to attack you right now; will you believe me?
blocks.30: The answer came in one voice, yes. We have never heard you tell a lie. The Prophet {{1}} said, then listen. I stand before you as a forewarner of a severe punishment.
blocks.31: He finished the statement. A tense silence fell. It was Abu Lahab who broke that silence. In the assembly he had not let the word be spoken at all. This time he could not stop it. The word was spoken; all Makkah had heard. Which of the two events came first and which later, there is a difference of opinion in the narrations of the Seerah. But that the man is the same, and the act is the same; about that there is no doubt.{{1}}
blocks.32: So this time he did not snatch the word. This time he abused. He shouted, ruin upon you all day long. Is this what you gathered us here for!{{1}}
blocks.33: His own uncle. A man of his own clan. On the very first day of the open da‘wah the first blow came from the nearest blood. The reply came down from the heavens
blocks.35: May the two hands of Abu Lahab perish, and he has perished indeed. His wealth and what he earned did not avail him. Soon he will enter a blazing fire. And his wife too, carrying firewood. Around her neck a rope of munj (a kind of grass).{{1}}
blocks.36: In the Qur’an he was called not by his real name; by his nickname. Abu Lahab. Father of the flame. But Islam did not give him this name. His own people had given him this nickname, long before prophethood. And they gave it in praise. His face was radiant. His cheeks glowed with a reddish hue. Seeing that glow people began to call him, father of the flame.{{1}}
blocks.37: That is, the name was a certificate of beauty. And the Qur’an did not change the name. It only changed the address of the flame. In the third verse of the surah it was said, he will soon enter a flaming fire. The very flame with which his face was praised became his address.
blocks.38: And why did the Qur’an not take the real name! ‘Abd al-‘Uzza. That is, the slave of the idol named al-‘Uzza. That name to be recited until the Day of Judgement, that cannot be. Abu Lahab was enormously rich. When frightened he would say, if my nephew’s words are true, then on the Day of Judgement I will get off with my wealth and children. The second verse of the surah is as if the reply to that; his wealth and his earnings were of no use to him at all.{{1}}
blocks.39: And his wife Umm Jamil bint Harb, the sister of Abu Sufyan; at night she would drag thorny branches and leave them on the path of the Prophet {{1}}. The Qur’an called her, the carrier of firewood.
blocks.40: Hearing that Surah Lahab was revealed, Umm Jamil ran out with a stone in her hand; to kill the Prophet {{1}}. The Prophet {{2}} was then sitting in the courtyard of the Ka‘bah with Abu Bakr (RA). Umm Jamil came and stood right in front, yet could not see the Prophet {{3}} at all; she saw only Abu Bakr. She asked, where is your companion? I have heard he is singing slanders about me. Then she recited a verse she had composed, we reject the reviled one, we disobey his command, we despise his religion. At the end she said, by Allah, if I had found him I would have crushed his head with this stone; I too am a poet. Saying this she left.
blocks.41: They would not call the Prophet {{1}} ‘Muhammad’ but ‘Mudhammam’; Muhammad means the praised one, Mudhammam means the reviled one. The Prophet {{2}} used to say, see how Allah turns away from me the abuse and curses of Quraysh! They abuse Mudhammam, they curse Mudhammam; and I am Muhammad.{{3}}
blocks.42: House to House, Market to Market
blocks.43: After the near relatives, now to everyone. The Prophet {{1}} stands in the courtyard of the Ka‘bah and recites the Qur’an. Goes into the crowd of the market and calls people. Goes from one door to another. When the Hajj season came, at ‘Ukaz, Majannah, Dhu al-Majaz; where the various tribes of Arabia pitched their tents, going from one tent to another he would say, O people, say La ilaha illa Allah, you will succeed.
blocks.44: And right behind him walked a man; Abu Lahab. Whatever the Prophet {{1}} said, he would say the opposite. He would say, do not listen to him, he is an apostate, he is a liar.{{2}}
blocks.45: One calling, another wanting to put out that call; this sight is now a daily one. But the word did not remain confined within the four walls of Makkah. The tribes that went back after Hajj said in their own areas, in Makkah a man has stood up, saying something new. The news went as far as Yathrib. It went toward Yemen, toward Najd, toward Ta’if. Wherever anyone returned, he returned carrying the word. The more Quraysh tried to stop it, the more the news spread.
blocks.46: The da‘wah was no longer secret. All Arabia came to know, in Makkah a man has stood up, who is calling to the One Allah. At home. In the marketplace. In the bazaar. At the fair. No separate gathering had to be arranged for the da‘wah.
blocks.47: We have tied the religion to one place. Religion in the mosque, religion on Friday. If talk of religion comes up sitting in a shop, it feels as if the place is not right. Yet he stood in the bazaar.
blocks.48: The Weapon That Sheds No Blood
blocks.49: Quraysh did not take up weapons at first. At first they took up the tongue.
blocks.51: One day they would call the Prophet {{1}} mad.
blocks.53: They say, O you upon whom this admonition (that is, the Qur’an) has been sent down, you are surely insane.{{1}}
blocks.54: Another day they would say sorcerer, liar. Hearing of the One Allah they would say in astonishment, he wants to trim so many gods down to one; this is a truly strange thing.{{1}}
blocks.55: About the Qur’an too various talk. Sometimes they said, these are the jumbled dreams that Muhammad sees at night in his sleep. Sometimes they said, he is fabricating it himself. Sometimes they said, a man teaches it to him.{{1}}
blocks.57: The most laughter came when they heard of the Hereafter. They said, we will die and become dust and bones, then stand up again? A poet composed a verse in mockery, did you hear! First death, then resurrection, then the Gathering; O Abu ‘Amr, this is mere superstition and fairy tale.{{1}}
blocks.58: Those Whose Whole Business Was Mockery
blocks.59: In Makkah there were a few whose very business was to mock the Prophet {{1}}; al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-‘As ibn Wa’il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, al-Aswad ibn ‘Abd Yaghuth, al-Harith ibn Qays. As soon as they saw the Prophet {{2}} they would twist their mouths, make signs, jeer behind his back.
blocks.60: Allah consoled the Prophet {{1}}, and took the responsibility for these upon His own shoulders
blocks.62: Rest assured, on your behalf your Lord alone is sufficient to settle matters with them, those who mock and ridicule (you).{{1}}
blocks.63: He said further, the messengers before you too were mocked; in the end that very mockery swallowed them up.{{1}}
blocks.64: That blow of the tongue has not stopped even today. A boy took up prayer. The first day no one said anything. Then he grew a beard. Then it began. Friends said, what, have you turned into a huzur (a religious cleric)! In the office someone said, backdated. Someone said in jest, careful, isn’t the boy turning into a militant! And what hurt the most came from home. His maternal uncle said, so his studies are gone.
blocks.65: No one beat him. No one tied him up. Only a few words were said. And with those few words alone he trimmed his beard short. The calculation is this. The Prophet {{1}} was called mad. He was called a sorcerer. He was called a liar. It was said, do not listen to him. And the one who heard these words did not move a hair’s breadth.
blocks.66: Let me tell of the girl too. She took up the hijab. Her friends said, we can’t even recognise you. One said, will the marriage happen now! Another said with a laugh, what need is there to be so good.
blocks.67: The name has changed. That day they said Mudhammam; reviled. Today they say backdated, extremist, overboard. But the work is one. The strategy is one. To turn the person into a laughing-stock. Because the one who is laughed at, no one weighs his words anymore.
blocks.68: And the Prophet {{1}} gave his reply in a different way. He did not go off angrily to quarrel. He said with a smile, see how Allah turns the abuse of Quraysh away from me! They abuse Mudhammam. And I am Muhammad.{{2}}
blocks.69: He did not take the abuse to heart. He changed the very name of the abuse. And what Allah said is for any person who is the target of mockery even today. He did not say, you give the reply. He said, I alone am sufficient for you against the mockers. That is, Allah has taken the work upon His own shoulders.
blocks.70: For the boy who trimmed his beard short, one word. Those who are laughing will not be there tomorrow. Walid laughed. ‘As ibn Wa’il laughed. Harith ibn Qays laughed. Today no one takes their names; if they do, it is only in connection with that laughter. And the one who was laughed at, his name rises to the sky five times a day.

footnotes.0: Surah al-Hijr, verse 94. After the revelation of this verse the Prophet {{1}} began the open da‘wah; the phase of secret da‘wah lasted about three years. In Tafsir Tawdih al-Qur’an too, in the note on this verse, it is said that this is the verse by which the command for open da‘wah came; before that the da‘wah was going on in secret.
footnotes.1: Surah al-Shu‘ara’, verse 214. The command to begin the open da‘wah first with the near relatives.
footnotes.2: Ibn Ishaq; Musnad Ahmad, hadith no. 1371 (via ‘Ali (RA)). On calling and feeding about forty of Banu Hashim and Banu ‘Abd al-Muttalib and giving them da‘wah. In the original Arabic narration the phrase is ‘badarahu Abu Lahab ila al-kalam’, that is, Abu Lahab spoke even before the Prophet {{1}} could speak; and his word ‘sorcery’ was about the blessing in the food just seen. The verifiers have called this chain of Musnad Ahmad weak; so the detailed scene of the courtyard gathering, especially the account of blessing in the small amount of food, is to be taken not as proof but as a narration of the Seerah. But the main event of giving da‘wah to the near relatives is sahih; see Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith no. 4770 and Sahih Muslim, hadith no. 208.
footnotes.3: How old ‘Ali (RA) was at this gathering is not specified in any narration; the narrations say only that he was the youngest of those present (Musnad Ahmad, hadith no. 1371). According to the narration of Ibn Ishaq his age at the time of accepting Islam was ten; in some narrations eight, nine, eleven, thirteen or even sixteen have come, but ten is the most famous. And this gathering was held in the fourth year of prophethood, after the revelation of verse 214 of Surah al-Shu‘ara’. On that reckoning his age comes to thirteen or fourteen. The number is not narrated; it is calculated.
footnotes.4: Ibn Ishaq; Sirat Ibn Hisham. On the standing up of only the youth ‘Ali (RA) in answer to the question ‘who will be my helper’ in the gathering of the near relatives. The narration is widely known in the Seerah books; it is not in Sahih al-Bukhari or Muslim.
footnotes.5: The gathering of the near relatives and the proclamation on the hill of Safa; both are reported to have happened after the revelation of verse 214 of Surah al-Shu‘ara’. In hadith no. 4770 of Sahih al-Bukhari the incident of Safa comes directly after the verse; and in the narrations of Ibn Ishaq and Musnad Ahmad the courtyard gathering comes. Most Seerah authors have placed the gathering first, but the order is not certain.
footnotes.6: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith no. 4770 (Book of Tafsir, Surah al-Shu‘ara’) and 4801; Sahih Muslim, hadith no. 208; via Ibn ‘Abbas (RA). On climbing the hill of Safa and calling clan by clan, the question ‘will you believe me’, the warning of punishment, and Abu Lahab’s saying ‘tabban laka’. The same incident has come in hadith no. 1394 of Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Funerals) too, but briefly; there only Abu Lahab’s statement and the revelation of Surah Lahab are mentioned, not the scene of Safa and the question and answer.
footnotes.7: Surah Lahab (Surah al-Masad), verses 1–5. Revealed in answer to Abu Lahab’s insult in the proclamation on the hill of Safa.
footnotes.8: The real name of Abu Lahab is ‘Abd al-‘Uzza ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib; ‘Abu Lahab’ was his kunyah or nickname, current since the Jahili period. The exegetes have mentioned that he was called by this name because of the radiance of his face and the reddish glow of his cheeks. See the tafsir of Imam al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, Surah Lahab; Sirat Ibn Hisham, on the lineage. This explanation about the derivation of the name is tafsir-based.
footnotes.9: On the occasion of revelation of verse 2 of Surah Lahab; on Abu Lahab’s saying ‘I will be saved with my wealth and children’. See Tafsir al-Tabari and Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Surah Lahab; Sirat al-Mustafa. The statement is mentioned in the tafsir books without a chain, in explanation of the verse. The statement of the verse, however, is definitive.
footnotes.10: Umm Jamil bint Harb’s coming with a stone, not being able to see the Prophet {{1}}, and her verse: Sirat Ibn Hisham 1/123; Sirat al-Mustafa; Tafsir Ibn Kathir, Surah Lahab. On ‘Mudhammam versus Muhammad’, Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith no. 3533; via Abu Hurayrah (RA).
footnotes.11: Musnad Ahmad, hadith no. 16023 and parallel narrations; via Rabi‘ah ibn ‘Ibbad al-Dili. On the open da‘wah of the Prophet {{1}} at Dhu al-Majaz and other Hajj seasons and Abu Lahab’s propaganda right behind him; Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut has called the narration sahih li-ghayrihi.
footnotes.12: Surah al-Hijr, verse 6. Quraysh used to call the Prophet {{1}} ‘mad’ (majnun).
footnotes.13: Surah Sad, verses 4–5. On the leaders of Quraysh calling the Prophet {{1}} ‘sorcerer, liar’ and calling the call to One God ‘a strange thing’. See Tafsir Ibn Kathir.
footnotes.14: The Qur’anic mention of the various sayings of the polytheists about the Qur’an: Surah al-Anbiya’, verse 5 (jumbled dreams); Surah al-Furqan, verse 4 (his own fabrication, others helped); Surah al-Nahl, verse 103 (a man teaches him).
footnotes.15: The Qur’anic mention of the statements of Quraysh denying the resurrection: Surah al-Saffat, verses 16–17; Surah Qaf, verse 3; Surah Saba’, verses 7–8. The verse of mockery (‘Did you hear! Death, resurrection, Gathering...’) is narrated in Sirat Ibn Hisham. The verse is quoted in Sirat Ibn Hisham without a chain; acceptable as a historical quotation. The verses, however, are the definitive statement of the Qur’an.
footnotes.17: Surah al-Hijr, verses 95–99 (the mockers and consolation of the Prophet {{1}}); Surah al-An‘am, verse 10 (even earlier prophets were mocked). The five chief mockers (al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-‘As ibn Wa’il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, al-Aswad ibn ‘Abd Yaghuth, al-Harith ibn Qays) and their ends: Sirat Ibn Hisham; al-Bayhaqi, Dala’il al-Nubuwwah. The detailed account of the names of the five and their ends has come in mursal and weak chains in the Dala’il of Ibn Ishaq and al-Bayhaqi. The names are famous in the Seerah, but the manner of their deaths is not established by sahih chains; so it is safer not to stress that account in the lesson. The verse ‘inna kafaynaka al-mustahzi’in’, however, is definitive.
footnotes.18: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith no. 3533; via Abu Hurayrah (RA). On the abuse as ‘Mudhammam’ and the reply of the Prophet {{1}}.

quiz.q: After the revelation of which verse did the Prophet ﷺ begin the open da‘wah?
o: Surah al-Hijr, verse 94
Surah al-‘Alaq, verse 1
Surah al-Muddaththir, verse 1
Surah al-Ma’idah, verse 3
quiz.e: After about three years of secret da‘wah, when verse 94 of Surah al-Hijr (‘proclaim openly what you have been commanded’) was revealed, the open da‘wah began.

quiz.q: With whom was the command to begin the open da‘wah first?
o: With all the chiefs of Makkah
With one’s own near relatives
With the inhabitants of Yathrib
With the outside tribes coming for Hajj
quiz.e: In verse 214 of Surah al-Shu‘ara’ the command was, ‘warn your near relatives’; so the da‘wah began first with Banu Hashim and the near ones.

quiz.q: What is the reason for beginning the open da‘wah with near relatives?
o: Because relatives would readily accept faith anyway
If one does not warn one’s own house, the call is weak, and the charge of favouritism also arises
Because permission to go to outsiders had not yet come
Because giving da‘wah among relatives was comparatively safe
quiz.e: If one cannot warn one’s own blood, the call to outsiders sounds weak; and again if relatives are warned, no one can say that he spared his own people.

quiz.q: Someone does not speak of religion at home and only preaches outside; what does this lesson remind him of?
o: Keeping away from the people of the house is safer
Going outside to preach is the more rewarding act
Da‘wah should begin from one’s own near ones
First many people, the family last of all
quiz.e: According to Surah al-Shu‘ara’ 214 the open da‘wah began with the near relatives; a call from outside that avoids one’s own house stands on a weak foundation.

quiz.q: From the command to begin the open da‘wah from home, what is the most direct lesson for today?
o: First tell the people of one’s own house
First tell the elders of the locality
First plan as a group
First tell outsiders
quiz.e: We give talks in the mosque, we do not give them at home; we write on Facebook, and the person lying in the next room we do not tell.

quiz.q: Why does our word sound hollow to the people at home, what does the lesson say?
o: People at home do not want to hear religion
People at home look at the speaker before the word
People at home already know everything
People at home have little time
quiz.e: Outsiders only hear the word; the people at home know whether the speaker gets up for Fajr or not.

quiz.q: What call did the Prophet ﷺ give on climbing the hill of Safa?
o: Allahu akbar
Hayya ‘ala al-salah
Ya Sabahah
Labbayka Allahumma
quiz.e: ‘Ya Sabahah’ was the early-morning danger signal the Arabs gave when an enemy suddenly fell upon them; at this very call everyone ran and gathered.

quiz.q: What answer did Quraysh give to the question ‘will you believe me’?
o: First show us a sign, then we will think
You are a man of our own tribe
We will have to think about this
We have never heard you tell a lie
quiz.e: Because of a lifetime of honesty they said without hesitation, ‘we have never heard you tell a lie’; right after this the Prophet ﷺ gave the warning of punishment.

quiz.q: Who interrupted the Prophet ﷺ in the proclamation on the hill of Safa with an insult?
o: Abu Lahab
Abu Jahl
‘Utbah ibn Rabi‘ah
Umayyah ibn Khalaf
quiz.e: His own uncle Abu Lahab said, ‘ruin upon you all day long; is this what you gathered us for’; the first blow of the open da‘wah came from the nearest blood.

quiz.q: In reply to Abu Lahab’s insult, which surah was revealed?
o: Surah al-Kafirun
Surah Lahab
Surah al-Kahf
Surah Quraysh
quiz.e: In reply to Abu Lahab’s insult in the proclamation of Safa, Surah Lahab was revealed, which speaks of the end of him and his wife.

quiz.q: Why is Abu Lahab called in the Qur’an by his nickname instead of his real name?
o: He himself had chosen this nickname by liking, it is regarded
Nobody in Makkah knew his real name then
A name meaning ‘slave of an idol’ is not fit to be kept in the Qur’an
The nickname was more current in his tribe and the market
quiz.e: ‘Abu Lahab’ means father of the flame, which fits his end; and the real name ‘Abd al-‘Uzza (slave of the idol al-‘Uzza) is not a name fit to be kept on the pages of the Qur’an.

quiz.q: What was Umm Jamil’s identity and her epithet in the Qur’an?
o: Mother of Abu Jahl; the Qur’an calls her accursed
Wife of Abu Talib; the Qur’an makes no mention
Daughter of ‘Utbah; her epithet in the Qur’an is proud
Wife of Abu Lahab; epithet carrier of firewood
quiz.e: Umm Jamil at night used to drag thorny branches and leave them on the path of the Prophet ﷺ; in Surah Lahab she is called ‘hammalat al-hatab’, that is, the carrier of firewood.

quiz.q: Why did the Prophet ﷺ give the example of ‘horsemen behind the hill’ at Safa?
o: To frighten Quraysh about a coming war
To display his eloquence before everyone
To take testimony of honesty from their own mouths before the talk of punishment
To explain why he had climbed the hill of Safa
quiz.e: By finding out whether they would believe him even on news of an unseen danger, he showed that his honesty was acknowledged by them; after that there is no argument left for denying the news of punishment.

quiz.q: What does it indicate that the first open opposition came from the nearest blood?
o: The remaining leaders of Quraysh were still neutral
Abu Lahab was a man of different temperament from before
The whole tribe of Banu Hashim went to the opposing side then
On the path of truth even ties of blood can become an obstacle
quiz.e: Abu Lahab’s opposition shows that on the path of da‘wah even the nearest relative can become an opponent; kinship is no guarantee of accepting the truth.

quiz.q: What lesson is there in the Qur’an not calling Abu Lahab by his real name?
o: Hiding a name makes the punishment of the Hereafter somewhat lighter
Calling someone by a nickname is more insulting than calling by the real name
The Qur’an never brings up anyone’s personal identity
A name meaning ‘slave of an idol’ is not fit to be kept in the Word of Allah
quiz.e: His nickname ‘father of the flame’ fits his end, and the real name meaning slave of an idol does not take its seat in the dignity of the Qur’an; even in choosing the name there is a message.

quiz.q: Someone says, ‘if I speak the truth, relatives will be angry’; what reply comes from this lesson?
o: Then delaying speaking the truth for some days is the wise thing
When their anger has subsided it can be said later at the right time
It is best not to tell relatives the truth at all
Even getting the first opposition from his uncle, the Prophet ﷺ did not stop
quiz.e: At the proclamation of Safa the first insult came from the mouth of his uncle Abu Lahab; yet the da‘wah did not stop. The displeasure of a relative is no excuse for hiding the truth.

quiz.q: What standard does this lesson set about one’s own character before giving da‘wah?
o: The speaker must be a skilled and good orator
The listeners should be able to say, ‘we have not heard him lie’
The speaker needs sufficient wealth in hand
The speaker’s lineage should be high
quiz.e: At Safa Quraysh themselves testified to his honesty; a trustworthy character built up beforehand is what makes the da‘wah acceptable.

quiz.q: Who ran propaganda right behind the Prophet ﷺ while he gave da‘wah in the Hajj season?
o: Abu Lahab
al-Nadr ibn al-Harith
al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah
‘Uqbah ibn Abi Mu‘ayt
quiz.e: In the narration of Rabi‘ah ibn ‘Ibbad, when the Prophet ﷺ said ‘say La ilaha illa Allah, you will succeed’, Abu Lahab walking right behind would say, ‘do not listen to him, he is a liar’.

quiz.q: What was the main means by which the da‘wah spread beyond the limits of Makkah to all Arabia?
o: Quraysh announced the whole matter in a written proclamation
The tribes returning after Hajj spread the news by word of mouth
Letters were passed hand to hand by trade caravans
The Jewish scholars of Madinah propagated it in their own area
quiz.e: The tribes coming in the season, after hearing the words of the Prophet ﷺ or hearing his name, would go back and spread them in their own area; in this way the news reached Yathrib and even farther.

quiz.q: In which verse does Allah assure the Prophet ﷺ about the mustahzi’un (the group of mockers)?
o: Surah al-Kahf, verse 23
Surah Lahab, verse 1
Surah al-Hijr, verse 95
Surah al-Kafirun, verse 6
quiz.e: ‘Surely, against the mockers I alone am sufficient for you’ (Surah al-Hijr 95); Allah takes upon His own shoulders the responsibility for their end.

quiz.q: Why did Quraysh at first choose mockery and slander rather than taking up weapons?
o: As a strategy to weaken the da‘wah while avoiding conflict
Because no enmity at all had yet arisen between them and the Prophet ﷺ
Because they had no weapons in hand then
Because his uncle Abu Talib had forbidden them to take up weapons
quiz.e: At the start, by laughter and mockery, slander and rumour, they wanted to break the morale of the Muslims and keep people away; the phase of torture comes later.

quiz.q: What the Prophet ﷺ did in reply to the abuse as ‘Mudhammam’, what is to be done today from it?
o: Silence them with a counter-reply
Get up and leave the assembly
Lodge a complaint about the matter at an appropriate place
Not take the abuse to heart, but set the name apart
quiz.e: He said, they abuse Mudhammam; and I am Muhammad. And Allah said, against the mockers I alone am sufficient.
